values: Does a hemorrhagic hepatic process require blood attenuation above 60 HU on NECT?

No. The article gives heterogeneous attenuation >60 HU as one possible appearance of hemorrhage; the melanoma example separately reports hemoperitoneum at 35 HU.
Pitfall: A single attenuation threshold must not exclude blood. Interpret attenuation with the lesion, sentinel clot and distribution of fluid.
Which CT approach is preferred for suspected hepatic trauma in a hemodynamically stable patient?

Dual-phase contrast CT. The AAST 2018 publication specifies arterial and portal venous phases to improve detection of vascular injury.
Report pivot: Assess active bleeding and its extent; distinguish blood already present in the peritoneum from active contrast extravasation into it.
Outside clarification: arterial-plus-portal-venous phase detail is from AAST 2018.
How does the location of active hepatic bleeding change the AAST 2018 CT vascular-injury grade?

Grade III vascular criterion: hepatic vascular injury or active bleeding contained within liver parenchyma.
Grade IV vascular criterion: active bleeding extends from the liver into the peritoneum.
Report pivot: Describe the bleeding compartment; other injuries may assign a higher grade. Hemoperitoneum alone is not the grade-IV active-bleeding criterion.
How does subcapsular hepatic hematoma extent affect AAST CT grading?

Less than 10% of the liver surface: grade I. From 10% through 50%: grade II. More than 50%, or a ruptured subcapsular hematoma: grade III.
Report pivot: Describe surface involvement and rupture; use the highest applicable injury grade.
